attachments.insertion_landmark: tongue body (fanning out from apex to base) and hyoid body

actions: protrudes and depresses the tongue (its most inferior fibers)

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Largest of the extrinsic tongue muscles; forms the bulk of the tongue body. Clinically important as the main muscle preventing posterior tongue collapse/airway obstruction during sleep (its weakness/hypotonia is implicated in obstructive sleep apnea).
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Submental (submandibular) approach, patient supine with the head tilted back: transducer/needle entry is placed just under the chin, off the midline. Ultrasound guidance (with or without concurrent EMG) is recommended so the needle's insertion, trajectory and depth can be tracked before it reaches the genioglossus; a purely landmark-based variant places two percutaneous insertion points 25-30 mm posterior to the midline of the mandibular body and 15-20 mm apart from each other, aimed toward the tongue base.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Needle passes from skin through the submental soft tissue and the suprahyoid muscle group (geniohyoid, mylohyoid, and/or the digastric) before reaching genioglossus -- reported EMG-confirmed genioglossus activity at roughly 2 cm depth via a submental trajectory through the digastric.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: EMG activity during voluntary tongue protrusion (or, in dystonia, during the dystonic movement) confirms genioglossus placement; ultrasound tracks the needle through the suprahyoid layer so it is not left in geniohyoid/mylohyoid/digastric.
structures_at_risk: suprahyoid muscles (geniohyoid, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric) in the needle path -- inadvertent injection here, or excessive genioglossus dose, is the main mechanism for post-injection dysphagia and aspiration risk
lingual artery and hypoglossal nerve, deeper/more posterior in the floor of mouth
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Reported for lingual dystonia (tongue protrusion type, the most common pattern) and, in a much narrower literature, an animal (rabbit) model of obstructive sleep apnea produced by paralyzing the genioglossus with intramuscular BoNT-A -- genioglossus weakness/paralysis is a mechanism of OSA rather than a treatment target, so BoNT is not used clinically for OSA. For lingual dystonia the submandibular route is injected at one or two sites, bilaterally; average dose per lingual-muscle injection reported around 43 U (range 15-60 U per session), titrated to EMG findings and response, with mild transient dysphagia the main (~12% of patients, ~4% of injections) side effect.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Yoshida K, 'Botulinum Neurotoxin Therapy for Lingual Dystonia Using an Individualized Injection Method Based on Clinical Features', Toxins (Basel) 11(1):51 (2019), doi:10.3390/toxins11010051 -- retrieved via PubMed; Rosales RL, Endaya NJ, 'The tongue muscles: Clinical applications in lingual dystonia', Toxicon 262:108382 (2025), doi:10.1016/j.toxicon.2025.108382 -- retrieved via PubMed.
